extracted.intended_audience: plant breeders, intellectual property attorneys, and IP professionals interested in U.S. plant protection law
extracted.subtask_short: PVPA protection for asexually reproduced plants
extracted.subtask_description: Explain the 2018 Farm Bill amendments to the Plant Variety Protection Act (PVPA) that make asexually reproduced plant varieties eligible for PVPA protection, and the related eligibility, infringement, labeling, and procedural rules applicants must consider.

rubrics_metrics.name: ASEXUALLY REPRODUCED — statutory definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The term “asexually reproduced” means produced by a method of plant propagation using vegetative material (other than seed) from a single parent, including cuttings, grafting, tissue culture, and propagation by root division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory definition (7 U.S.C. §2401(a)(1)) determines which varieties qualify as asexually reproduced for PVPA eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: PVPA eligibility — entitlement to protection (statutory threshold)
rubrics_metrics.description: The breeder of any sexually reproduced, tuber propagated, or asexually reproduced plant variety (other than fungi or bacteria) who has so reproduced the variety, or the successor in interest of the breeder, shall be entitled to plant variety protection for the variety, subject to the conditions and requirements of this chapter, if the variety is— (1) new … (2) distinct … (3) uniform … (4) stable … (7 U.S.C. §2402(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes who may apply and the four core substantive requirements (new, distinct, uniform, stable) that must be met for a certificate to issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty ('new') requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The variety must be new in the sense that prior to the application filing 'propagating or harvested material of the variety has not been sold or otherwise disposed of to other persons, by or with the consent of the breeder, or the successor in interest of the breeder, for purposes of exploitation of the variety,' as set forth in 7 U.S.C. §2402(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sales (including sale of cut flowers or hybrid seed harvested from a variety) can bar PVPA protection unless within statutory grace periods. The PVPA affords a one-year grace period for sales or disposition by or on behalf of the breeder as part of experimentation/testing or to increase the variety; and four- and six-year grace periods for sales/exploitation outside the U.S. for non-woody and woody species respectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctness requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The variety must be 'distinct' (statutory term listed in 7 U.S.C. §2402(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute requires distinctness as a condition of protection; the article does not recite test details but treats 'distinct' as one of the four statutory substantive requirements for PVPA certificates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The variety must be 'uniform' (statutory term listed in 7 U.S.C. §2402(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniformity is a statutory requirement for PVPA protection; specific testing/measurement protocols are expected to be set out in PVPO rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The variety must be 'stable' (statutory term listed in 7 U.S.C. §2402(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stability is a statutory requirement for PVPA protection; PVPO rulemaking will likely clarify evidence/specimen requirements to demonstrate stability for asexually reproduced varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions — fungi and bacteria
rubrics_metrics.description: PVPA entitlement excludes fungi or bacteria (7 U.S.C. §2402(a) parenthetical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants working with fungi or bacteria cannot obtain PVPA protection under the amended statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts constituting infringement (scope of exclusive rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: Except as otherwise provided in this subchapter, it shall be an infringement ... to perform without authority ... sexually or asexually multiply, or propagate by a tuber or a part of a tuber, the variety as a step in marketing (for growing purposes) the variety (7 U.S.C. §2541(a)(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes core infringing acts under PVPA for protected varieties; it defines reproduction/propagation and certain marketing-related multiplication as infringing before expiration of protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited marketing/labeling practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of the following acts, if performed in connection with the sale, offering for sale, or advertising of sexually or asexually reproducible plant material or tubers or parts of tubers, is prohibited: (1) Use of the words 'U.S. Protected Variety' or any word or number importing that the material is a variety protected under certificate, when it is not. (2) Use of any wording importing that the material is a variety for which an application for plant variety protection is pending, when it is not. (3) Use of either the phrase 'Unauthorized Propagation Prohibited' or 'Unauthorized Seed Multiplication Prohibited' or similar phrase without reasonable basis. Any reasonable basis expires one year after the first sale of the variety except as justified thereafter by a pending application or a certificate still in force. (4) Failure to use the name of a variety for which a certificate of protection has been issued under this chapter, even after the expiration of the certificate, except that certain grass and forage seeds may be sold without a variety name unless state law requires it (7 U.S.C. §2568(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These labeling/advertising prohibitions can trigger PVPO cease-and-desist orders after hearing; they set specific limits on claims about protected status and the use of 'Unauthorized' legend language without a continuing reasonable basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term of protection
rubrics_metrics.description: The term of protection is 20 and 25 years from date of issue for non-woody and woody species, respectively (7 U.S.C. §2483).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PVPA term is measured from date of issue (not date of filing, as with plant patents for which term is 20 years from filing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential derivation / predominance / essential characteristics standard
rubrics_metrics.description: New varieties generally remain subject to the rights of the owner of the initial variety if they are predominantly derived from a protected variety, are clearly distinguishable from the protected variety, and conform to the protected variety in the expression of essential characteristics resulting from the genotype or combination of genotypes of the protected variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'essential derivation' framework gives original breeders a metric of similarity to prevent effective copying of germplasm while leaving room for wholly new varieties; it is the PVPA's mechanism to limit breeders' exceptions and protect against downstream products that are essentially the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison to Plant Patent Act — scope of protection and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Plant Patent Act, a breeder with a U.S. plant patent could only exclude others from asexually reproducing the protected variety, and from using, offering for sale, or selling plants or any parts derived therefrom; others were free to use the protected variety to generate new varieties (including via mutation, gene-editing, or introduction of exogenous genetic material) so long as they avoided asexual reproduction of the protected variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This highlights the practical differences between plant patents and PVPA protection: PVPA (with essential-derivation concepts) can reach certain downstream varieties that are predominantly derived, while plant patents historically allowed more freedom to create new varieties from protected material provided the new variety was not asexual reproduction of the protected variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specimen deposit and application requirements — anticipated PVPO rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. Plant Variety Protection Office (PVPO) is expected to issue proposed changes to the rules to implement the Plant Variety Protection Act; breeders are awaiting adoption of the new rules to clarify application requirements, including specimen deposit requirements, which are certain to differ from those imposed on sexually-reproduced plants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural requirements (e.g., what specimens to deposit for asexually reproduced varieties, how to demonstrate uniformity/stability) will be set out in PVPO regulations; applicants should monitor PVPO rulemaking before filing to ensure compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical factors favoring PVPA over a plant patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Situations where pursuing PVPA protection may benefit asexually reproduced varieties: if the variety has been sold outside the U.S. more than one year ago, a plant patent is barred, but one could still file for PVPA protection if the sale was an integral part of a testing program by or on behalf of the breeder or the sale is within four years or six years (for trees/vines) of the sale. Also, PVPA protection is generally longer than plant patent protection (20/25 years from issue versus 20 years from filing for plant patents), and PVPA offers breeders' exceptions not available under plant patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are practical selection criteria for deciding whether to pursue PVPA vs plant patent protection for an asexually reproduced variety based on prior sales, term length, and available breeder exceptions.
